title: Solutions and solubility
summary: Learn about dissolving, concentration units, colligative properties and solubility.
cards.0.p: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. The substance that spreads out is called the solute, and the substance it spreads into is the solvent. Like dissolves like. That's why polar ethanol and water mix in any proportion.
cards.0.key: Ethanol and water form hydrogen bonds. In an aqueous solution, (aq) is written after the solute, for example NaCl(aq).
cards.0.once.soru: Why doesn't oil dissolve in water?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.yazi: Oil is nonpolar, water is polar
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Like dissolves like. Nonpolar oil doesn't interact with polar water.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Being lighter doesn't decide solubility. Ethanol is also lighter than water, but it dissolves in water.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Liquid oils don't dissolve in water either.
cards.1.p: Ionic solids such as NaCl split into ions in water. Sugar spreads out as molecules. Particles being surrounded by water molecules is called hydration. Dissolving is a physical change.
cards.1.svg#3: O end (δ−) turns to the ion
cards.1.svg#4: H ends (δ+) turn to the ion
cards.1.key: If the solvent is not water, this is called solvation. Salt water conducts electricity because it contains ions, but sugar water does not.
cards.2.p: In dissolving, energy is absorbed as the particles separate and released as the solvent surrounds them. Depending on which is larger, dissolving is exothermic or endothermic.
cards.2.key: When NaOH and H₂SO₄ dissolve, the container warms. When NH₄NO₃ and KNO₃ dissolve, the container cools. Substances that dissolve endothermically become more soluble with temperature.
cards.2.once.soru: When the salt in a cold pack dissolves in water, the pack gets cold. What kind of dissolving is this?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Dissolving takes heat from the surroundings. That's why the pack gets cold.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: If it were exothermic, the pack would warm up.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Dissolving is a physical change, and no new substance forms.
cards.3.p: Mass percent is the mass of solute in 100 g of solution. For example, a solution of 20 g of salt and 80 g of water is 20%. For very dilute solutions, ppm is used. 1 ppm means 1 mg of solute in 1 kg of solution.
cards.3.svg#0: Expressing concentration as percent and ppm
cards.3.svg#22: ppm: parts per million; for very dilute solutions
cards.3.key: The denominator is the solution, not the solvent. Volume percent is used for liquids. 100 mL of an 80% cologne contains 80 mL of ethanol.
cards.4.p: Molarity is the number of moles of solute in 1 liter of solution, found from M = n / V. Here V is the volume of the solution, not of the solvent.
cards.4.etk.soru: M = n / V. Change the mass of solute, the molar mass and the final volume of the solution. (NaOH: 40 g/mol)
cards.4.key: For example, 4 g of NaOH (40 g/mol) is 0.1 mol. If it is made up to 250 mL with water, the concentration is 0.1 / 0.25 = 0.4 M. Don't forget to convert mL to liters.
cards.5.p: Molality is the number of moles of solute per 1 kg of solvent, and it doesn't change with temperature. Mole fraction is the moles of one component divided by the total moles, and it has no unit.
cards.5.key: Molarity is based on liters of solution, and molality on kilograms of solvent.
cards.5.once.soru: Which one doesn't change when a solution is heated?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Molality is based on mass, and mass doesn't change with heat.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The volume expands with heat, so the molarity drops slightly.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Molality is based on mass, so it stays constant.
cards.6.p: If you add water to a solution, the moles don't change, only the volume grows. So M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. If two solutions are mixed, add up the moles and divide by the total volume.
cards.6.key: The concentration of a mixture is Mfinal = (M₁V₁ + M₂V₂) / (V₁ + V₂). Mixing equal volumes of 1 M and 3 M solutions gives 2 M.
cards.7.h: From percent and density to molarity
cards.7.p: A bottle of concentrated acid lists the mass percent and the density. The molarity is M = 10·d·% / MA. For example, 36.5% HCl (d = 1.2 g/mL) is 12 M.
cards.7.key: MA is the molar mass. In the formula, the percent is written as a number (36.5) and d in g/mL.
cards.7.once.soru: What is the mass in grams of 1 L of a solution with density 1.2 g/mL?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The mass of 1 L of solution is 1000 mL × 1.2 g/mL = 1200 g.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is the mass of 1 mL. 1 L is 1000 mL.
cards.8.p: When an ionic substance dissociates, the concentration of each ion equals the salt concentration times its coefficient in the formula. For example, in 1 M CaCl₂, [Ca²⁺] = 1 M and [Cl⁻] = 2 M.
cards.8.key: Square brackets show molar concentration. If solutions with a common ion are mixed, add up that ion's moles and divide by the total volume.
cards.9.p: Some properties depend not on the kind of solute but on the number of particles. These are called colligative properties. When a nonvolatile substance dissolves, the vapor pressure drops (Raoult's law).
cards.9.svg#4: Raoult: P = X · P° (X: mole fraction of solvent)
cards.9.key: Raoult's law is P = Xsolvent·P°solvent. Boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure are also colligative properties.
cards.9.once.soru: Sugar water and salt water have the same concentration. Which has the lower vapor pressure?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: NaCl gives two ions. More particles lower the vapor pressure more.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Sugar doesn't ionize and gives fewer particles.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The concentration is the same, but the number of particles differs.
cards.10.p: A solution of a nonvolatile substance freezes at a lower temperature and boils at a higher temperature than pure water. The change is ΔT = K·m·i, where i is the number of particles. i = 1 for sugar, 2 for NaCl and 3 for CaCl₂.
cards.10.svg#0: Water and 1 m NaCl solution at 1 atm
cards.10.key: Because the vapor pressure is lower, it reaches the outside pressure at a higher temperature. Antifreeze added to engine coolant prevents freezing the same way.
cards.11.p: Water moves through a semipermeable membrane from the dilute side to the concentrated side. This is called osmosis. The pressure that stops this flow is called osmotic pressure. Applying more pressure to the concentrated side is called reverse osmosis.
cards.11.svg#8: - - - semipermeable membrane: water passes, ions don't
cards.11.key: Reverse osmosis makes seawater drinkable. What passes through the membrane is water, not the solute. Saline solution has the same osmotic pressure as blood.
cards.11.once.soru: What happens if you soak a cucumber in salt water?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The outside is more concentrated. So water leaves the cucumber.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Water moves to the concentrated side, which is outside.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: There is a concentration difference between inside and outside. So water moves.
cards.12.p: Solubility is the most substance that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. A solution that reaches this limit is saturated, and one below it is unsaturated.
cards.12.key: Tables usually give solubility in g per 100 g of water. For gases the pressure is also stated. A hot saturated solution that is cooled carefully can hold the extra solute for a while. This is called a supersaturated solution.
cards.12.once.soru: At 20 °C, 100 g of water dissolves at most 36 g of salt. What happens if you add 50 g of salt?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: 36 g dissolves, and the excess (14 g) stays undissolved.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: At that temperature water can't dissolve more than 36 g.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: 36 g, up to the limit, dissolves.
cards.13.p: The solubility of solids usually rises with temperature. The solubility of gases falls with temperature and rises with pressure (Henry's law). A common ion also lowers solubility.
cards.13.svg#11: Pressure has practically no effect on solids and liquids.
cards.13.key: There are exceptions such as Ca(OH)₂. AgCl dissolves less in NaCl solution than in pure water. In hot summers, dissolved oxygen in lakes decreases.
cards.14.p: The curve shows the most substance 100 g of water can dissolve at each temperature. When a hot saturated solution is cooled, the excess substance comes out as crystals.
cards.14.key: At 60 °C, 110 g of KNO₃ dissolves in 100 g of water, and at 20 °C, 32 g. So when the solution cools, 78 g of KNO₃ comes out. With 200 g of water, twice as much would come out.
cards.15.p:
• Like dissolves like. Dissolving can absorb or release heat.
• Concentration is expressed as percent, ppm, molarity (M = n/V), molality and mole fraction.
• In dilution the moles stay constant: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
• Colligative properties depend on the number of particles (ΔT = K·m·i).
• Solubility depends on temperature and, for gases, on pressure.
quiz.0.q: The solubility of KNO₃ is 110 g at 60 °C and 32 g at 20 °C per 100 g of water. A saturated solution made with 50 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. How many grams of KNO₃ come out?
quiz.0.e: 50 g of water dissolves 55 g of KNO₃ at 60 °C and 16 g at 20 °C. The difference is 55 − 16 = 39 g.
quiz.1.q: Order the freezing points at 1 atm from highest to lowest.
quiz.1.e: Freezing point depression is ΔT = K·m·i and depends on the number of particles. Pure water has no depression. i = 1 for sugar, 2 for NaCl and 3 for CaCl₂. So the CaCl₂ solution freezes at the lowest temperature.
quiz.2.q: 200 mL of 0.5 M NaCl is mixed with 300 mL of 1 M NaCl. What is the concentration of the final solution in M? (Volumes add up.)
quiz.2.e: Add up the moles: 0.2·0.5 + 0.3·1 = 0.4 mol. The total volume is 0.5 L, so the concentration is 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8 M.
quiz.3.q: A student says, "As temperature rises, every substance becomes more soluble in water." Which is true about this claim?
quiz.3.o.1: It is true for every substance.
quiz.3.o.2: It is true only at constant pressure.
quiz.3.e: The solubility of solids usually rises, but that of gases falls with temperature (and so does that of some solids such as Ca(OH)₂). Also, the rate of dissolving and solubility are not the same thing.
quiz.3.y.1: Rate and solubility are different ideas. As temperature rises, gases escape from water and their solubility falls.
quiz.3.y.2: Even at constant pressure, the solubility of gases falls as temperature rises. So the generalization is wrong.
quiz.3.y.3: Temperature does affect solubility. It raises the solubility of most solids and lowers that of gases.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Dissolve salt, set the concentration, dilute the solution and freeze it.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Add sugar to the water first, then salt. Watch the dissolved particles and the bulb in the circuit.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Why does salt water conduct electricity?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Pure water has very few ions and doesn't light the bulb. In sugar water the bulb stayed dim too.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water (ionic dissolving). Sugar spreads out as molecules and gives no ions (molecular dissolving). Substances that split into ions in water and make the solution conduct are called electrolytes.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The crystal breaks apart in water. Water molecules surround the ions and pull them apart. An undissolved crystal couldn't carry charge.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Mass percent is the mass of solute divided by the mass of solution, times 100. The glass holds 20 g of salt. Adjust the water and make the solution 40% by mass.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 20 g of salt and 30 g of water make 50 g of solution. 20 / 50 = 40%. The denominator is again the mass of the solution. If you had divided by the water, you'd get 67%.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Molarity is the number of moles divided by the volume of solution in liters. The flask holds 0.1 mol of NaOH. Change the volume to make the solution 0.5 M.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: V = n / M = 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 L, that is 200 mL. The same amount of substance in a smaller volume is more concentrated.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You have 100 mL of a 2 M solution. Add water to bring the concentration to 0.8 M.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: Adding water doesn't change the moles, so there is always 0.2 mol. Since 2 · 100 = 0.8 · V₂, V₂ = 250 mL. So you added 150 mL of water.
A:adimlar.4.metin: CaCl₂ splits into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions in water. Change the concentration and watch the ion bars.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What is the total ion concentration in a 0.5 M CaCl₂ solution?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That is only the Ca²⁺ concentration. Each CaCl₂ also gives two Cl⁻.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That is only the Cl⁻ concentration (2 · 0.5). You need to add the Ca²⁺ ions too.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: CaCl₂ splits into Ca²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ in water. [Ca²⁺] = 0.5 M and [Cl⁻] = 1 M, so the total is 1.5 M. One formula unit gives 3 ions.
A:adimlar.5.metin: We put pure water, sugar water, salt water (NaCl) and a CaCl₂ solution in the freezer. All are 1 molal.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Of the solutions, which freezes last?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Sugar doesn't ionize, and each molecule stays as one particle (i = 1). So the freezing point drops by only 1.86 °C.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: NaCl gives two ions (i = 2), and the freezing point drops by 3.72 °C. But there is a solute that gives three ions.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3), so this solution has the most particles. The freezing point drops by 1.86 · 3 ≈ 5.6 °C. That's why salt is spread on roads in winter.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Soda contains CO₂ dissolved under pressure. Open the cap, change the temperature and watch the dissolved CO₂ bar.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Why does soda fizz when you open it?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Opening the cap doesn't change the soda's temperature. And the bubbles are CO₂, not water vapor.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Air gets in and forms bubbles
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The bubbles are not air from outside, but CO₂ leaving the liquid.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A gas's solubility is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid (Henry's law). When the cap opens, the pressure drops and the extra CO₂ comes out as bubbles.
A:adimlar.7.metin: We put 100 g of water in a beaker. Add KNO₃ (potassium nitrate) and change the temperature. Dissolved ions spread through the water, and the undissolved part stays at the bottom as crystals. Look at the dot on the right and the solubility curve. Find the following yourself.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Add KNO₃ to the water at 20 °C. What is the most that dissolves?
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: At 20 °C, about 32 g of KNO₃ dissolved in 100 g of water and the rest stayed at the bottom. This solution is saturated, meaning it can't dissolve more KNO₃ at that temperature.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Dissolve the solid at the bottom by heating (with at least 40 g of KNO₃).
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The solubility of KNO₃ rises quickly with temperature, and at 45 °C all 50 g dissolved. Most solids behave this way. Gases, though, dissolve less when hot.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: With everything dissolved, cool the solution below 25 °C and watch the bottom.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: As it cooled, the solubility fell and the extra KNO₃ came out as crystals. Dissolving when hot and cooling to get pure crystals is called recrystallization.
A:kapanis.0: Salt splits into ions in water and its solution conducts electricity. Sugar spreads out as molecules.
A:kapanis.1: Mass percent is the mass of solute divided by the mass of the solution. Molarity is M = n / V, with V in liters.
A:kapanis.2: In dilution the moles don't change: M₁·V₁ = M₂·V₂. To find an ion's concentration, multiply the salt concentration by that ion's count in the formula.
A:kapanis.3: Colligative properties depend on the number of particles (ΔT = K·m·i). The more ions, the lower the freezing point.
A:kapanis.4: The solubility of gases rises with pressure and falls with temperature.
